props.title: Faster, Pussycat! Kill! Kill!
props.initialSlug: Three go-go dancers embark on a violent crime spree

sections.content: Faster, Pussycat! Kill! Kill! revolutionized exploitation cinema through Russ Meyer's distinct vision of powerful women and high-octane action. Led by Tura Satana's iconic performance as Varla, this desert-set thriller follows three go-go dancers on a violent crime spree. Meyer's rapid-fire editing and dynamic camera angles created a visual language that influenced directors from Kill Bill (2003) to Death Proof (2007). John Waters called it the best movie ever made, and Quentin Tarantino regularly cites it as a major influence.

sections.content: Meyer's influence extends far beyond exploitation cinema. His rapid editing techniques and extreme close-ups created a distinctive visual style that influenced music video aesthetics of the 1980s. Mad Max: Fury Road (2015) echoes Meyer's desert-bound action and powerful female characters, while Planet Terror (2007) directly homages his exploitation style.

The film's feminist undertones, though controversial, challenged 1960s gender roles through its portrayal of physically dominant women. While modern viewers might question some elements, its impact on female action roles remains significant, paving the way for films like Ms .45 (1981) and Lady Snowblood (1973). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Modern Influence

Contemporary filmmakers continue drawing from Meyer's playbook. Drive Angry (2011) and Machete (2010) channel similar high-octane exploitation energy, while art house films like The Love Witch (2016) reference Meyer's saturated visual style and gender commentary.
